lead: At a post-tensioned anchorage, a jack force of hundreds or thousands of kilonewtons enters the concrete through a small steel plate. The force cannot stay concentrated: it spreads out into the end block and then into the full beam. This spreading produces transverse tension behind the plate, called bursting. A separate local effect, called spalling, appears in the concrete around the plate at the loaded face, because the stiff plate restrains the lateral expansion of the concrete beneath it; this tension acts on planes parallel to the loaded face, just outside the plate. Both must be dealt with, but they have different causes. The end block must have enough bearing area and transverse reinforcement to carry these local effects. The same idea appears at every post-tensioned anchor in a bridge, a parking slab or a metro viaduct segment.
prereq: You need: 6.1 and 6.3; post-tensioning introduces the concentrated anchorage force.

blocks.text: An anchorage zone is the region near a post-tensioning anchor where the tendon force enters the concrete. It has two parts. The primary zone is the small block immediately behind the bearing plate. Here the force is still concentrated, bearing stress is high, and spalling tension can appear near the loaded face. The secondary zone is the larger end block where the force spreads from the plate area to the full concrete section. This spreading produces transverse bursting tension. The primary zone is controlled mainly by bearing plate size and local mesh; the secondary zone is controlled by closed stirrups or similar transverse steel. Pre-tensioned members transfer force by bond over a length, so this end-block problem belongs mainly to post-tensioning, discussed in 6.3.

The first check is bearing. A plate of area A<sub>plate</sub> presses on concrete with average stress σ<sub>b</sub> = P / A<sub>plate</sub>. P is the anchorage force after losses, in newtons; A<sub>plate</sub> is the net plate area in mm²; σ<sub>b</sub> is bearing stress in N/mm². Use the same force units throughout. A 1000 kN force is 1,000,000 N, not 1000 N. The plate must be large enough that σ<sub>b</sub> does not exceed the permitted bearing stress for the concrete. Concrete under a plate is confined by the surrounding concrete, so its bearing strength is higher than its cube strength, but this benefit is limited. A thin plate can bend or punch into concrete, so plate thickness and stiffness matter too. If σ<sub>b</sub> is too high, enlarge the plate or use a stronger concrete; adding stirrups alone does not fix bearing.

blocks.where: σ<sub>b</sub> is average bearing stress in N/mm²; P is anchorage force in N; A<sub>plate</sub> is plate area in mm².

blocks.text: Behind the plate the force spreads outward, like water from a narrow nozzle. The spreading lines of force pull the concrete sideways and create transverse tension. For a square or rectangular plate, an approximate bursting force is F<sub>bst</sub> ≈ 0.25 P (1 − a/b). Here P is the anchorage force after losses, the jack force reduced by losses, and the same value is used for both the bearing check and the bursting check. a is the plate width in the direction considered, and b is the end-block width in the same direction; a/b is dimensionless. The force F<sub>bst</sub> is in the same units as P. A wider plate gives a smaller 1 − a/b and less bursting. For a rectangular plate, repeat the bursting check in both directions, taking a and b in the same direction each time, and provide stirrups for the bursting force found in each direction. The bursting force is not flexural steel demand; it is a splitting force inside the end block. Provide closed stirrups, U-bars or spirals around the tendon, spread over the bursting zone, with area A<sub>st</sub> ≈ F<sub>bst</sub> / (0.87 f<sub>y</sub>), with F<sub>bst</sub> in N, f<sub>y</sub> in N/mm² and A<sub>st</sub> in mm². Convert F<sub>bst</sub> from kN to N before using the formula: 166.7 kN = 166,700 N. Place several small layers rather than one heavy layer, and anchor them well. Near the surface, add a light mesh for spalling.

items: Place closed stirrups around the duct, starting close to the plate.
Spread them over the bursting zone, roughly one member depth.
Add surface mesh or small U-bars for spalling near the loaded face.
Keep the bearing plate concentric with the tendon.

figure.caption: A jack force passes through a bearing plate and spreads into the end block, producing transverse bursting tension that closed stirrups resist.

spec.title: Anchorage zone action
spec.aria: A jack force passes through a bearing plate and spreads into the end block, producing transverse bursting tension that needs closed stirrups.

examples.question: An anchorage force P = 1000 kN acts on a square plate 200 mm × 200 mm at the end of a beam 600 mm wide. Find the bearing stress and an approximate bursting force.
steps: P is the anchorage force after losses. Convert it: P = 1000 kN = 1000 × 1000 = 1,000,000 N.
Bearing stress: σ<sub>b</sub> = P / A<sub>plate</sub> = 1,000,000 / 40,000 = 25 N/mm².
Take plate width a = 200 mm and end-block width b = 600 mm. Then a/b = 200/600 = 0.333.

Bursting force: F<sub>bst</sub> ≈ 0.25 P (1 − a/b) = 0.25 × 1000 × (1 − 0.333) = 250 × 0.667 = 166.7 kN. For stirrup area, use this as 166,700 N in A<sub>st</sub> = F<sub>bst</sub> / (0.87 f<sub>y</sub>).
examples.answer: The bearing stress is 25 N/mm² and the approximate bursting force is 166.7 kN. The same P after losses is used for both checks.
examples.check:
P_kN = 1000
a = 200
b = 600
P_N = P_kN * 1000
A_plate = a * a
sigma_b = P_N / A_plate
F_bst = 0.25 * P_kN * (1 - a / b)
print(round(sigma_b, 1))
print(round(F_bst, 1))

traps: Designing end-block steel as flexural steel. It resists transverse splitting, so flexural formulas and lever arms do not apply.
Using P in kN with plate area in mm² and calling the result N/mm². Convert P to newtons first.
Taking b as the beam depth when checking bursting across the width. a and b must be plate and end-block widths in the same direction.
Checking only bursting and forgetting bearing stress and spalling; all three belong to end-block design.
Assuming a wider plate always removes the need for stirrups; it reduces bursting but does not eliminate local tension.

quiz.q: Write the formula for average bearing stress under an anchorage plate and define each term.
quiz.a: σ<sub>b</sub> = P / A<sub>plate</sub>, where P is the anchorage force in N, A<sub>plate</sub> is the plate area in mm², and σ<sub>b</sub> is bearing stress in N/mm².

quiz.q: Why does a concentrated anchorage force create transverse tension in the end block?
quiz.a: The force enters through a small plate and spreads out to the full section. The spreading lines of force pull the concrete sideways, producing transverse bursting tension behind the plate.

quiz.q: P = 800 kN acts on a square plate 150 mm × 150 mm. The end-block width is b = 500 mm. Find the bearing stress and approximate bursting force.
A designer increases the plate size but keeps the same P. Explain the effect on bearing stress and bursting force.
quiz.a: A larger plate increases A<sub>plate</sub>, so bearing stress P/A<sub>plate</sub> falls. It also increases a/b, so the factor (1 − a/b) falls and the approximate bursting force 0.25P(1 − a/b) falls. Local spalling near the plate edge still needs attention.

quiz.q: What is spalling and where does it occur?
quiz.a: Spalling is local surface tension near the loaded face, outside or around the bearing plate. It can break off a thin concrete cover, so small mesh or U-bars are placed near the anchorage.

quiz.q: Why is it wrong to design end-block stirrups as flexural reinforcement?
quiz.a: End-block stirrups carry transverse splitting tension caused by force spreading, not bending moment. Flexural steel is placed where bending tension acts and uses a lever arm. End-block steel must surround the tendon and be distributed over the bursting zone.

beyond: Not for the exam. In practice, end-block design is checked with strut-and-tie models and finite element analysis, especially where several tendons anchor close together. Search for 'anchorage zone bursting force post-tensioned concrete' and 'strut-and-tie end block'. Modern bridge manuals give anchorage zone reinforcement details for large tendon groups. Bearing plate optimisation and ductile end-zone detailing remain active design topics.
